body: Coverage in Jordan is taken by a black Google car without a red brake light or antenna, unique in the Middle East.
Jordanian license plates are white, long or short, with a distinctive green strip on the left for commercial vehicles. The green strip is exclusive to Jordan within the Middle East.
The official language used in Jordan is Arabic, identifiable by its lines and dots. Unlike the UAE, most commercial signs in Jordan lack English text.
Roads in Jordan typically feature yellow outside lines and white middle lines. Similar road line styles are found in other Middle Eastern countries.
Jordan's chevrons are white with red arrows. Israeli chevrons are black with white arrows, useful for distinction.
Typical Jordanian electricity poles include round concrete poles with diagonal supports or three horizontal Y-shaped tops, and thin metal poles with vertical coils.
Jordan's landscape is very arid, with sparse vegetation and mostly desert scenery, giving even lush areas a dry Mediterranean appearance.
Most buildings in Jordan are constructed with bright sandstone bricks and flat roofs. The same sandstone material can also be seen in Jerusalem and the West Bank.
Road conditions in Jordan vary; some roads, especially those in poor condition, show warping and cracking caused by heat. Overall, road quality is generally worse than in Israel.
Street View coverage in Jordan is limited to the far western part, mainly larger towns and main roads. It ends just north of Jerash, with no coverage in Irbid, and extends south to Aqaba.
Amman is the largest city with extensive coverage; a bustling, hilly metropolis with medium-sized apartment blocks.
Highway 15, the longest divided highway, runs through desert and rocky hills near Aqaba.
Highway 35 from Amman to Jerash features hills with green vegetation and T-shaped lampposts.
Highway 40, west of Amman, is a divided road through hilly terrain into the Dead Sea area, with Y-shaped lampposts along its length.
The Dead Sea is west of Highway 65's northern section, with a long, flat ridge opposite it.
Highway 65 south of Feifa Valley has long, sandy stretches with occasional overcast or sunset coverage near Aqaba.
Madaba has flat, tilled fields with rich, red soil that extend along Highway 35.
Wadi al Hasa valley features arid, rounded hills and a single-lane highway running through the center.
Highway 80 is a divided valley road with large mountains that become flatter near Aqaba, running east to west.
Jagged mountains east and south of Aqaba are visible in coverage.
Taxis in Amman are yellow and green; taxi colors help identify the city.
Aqaba taxis are olive green on top and black at the bottom.
Madaba taxis are yellow with white bumpers.
Petra's trekker coverage shows highly eroded reddish rocks, narrow gorges, and archaeological sites with tourist crowds.
